title: How Supermarkets Make Money on Tiny Margins

scenes.title: Cold open
scenes.chapter: A hundred dollars at the checkout

beats.narration: You hand over a hundred dollars at the checkout.
beats.visual: Checkout lane already moving at frame 0; a generic $100 bill slides in; question band on screen
on_screen_text: Of every $100 you spend at a supermarket… how much does the store keep?

beats.narration: Bread, coffee, a gallon of milk, a week of dinners. The scanner beeps, the receipt prints, and the money disappears into the register.
beats.visual: Bread, coffee, milk and a deli meal cross the scanner on the spoken words (beeps); register total climbs; receipt prints

beats.narration: So how much of that hundred dollars does the supermarket actually keep?
beats.visual: Close-up on the bill with a question badge
on_screen_text: How much does the supermarket keep?

beats.narration: At Kroger, which runs nearly 2,700 supermarkets across the United States, the answer for its latest fiscal year was about $1.28 in operating profit.
beats.visual: Bill shrinks to the left; 2,697 green squares fill in (one per supermarket); $1.28 counts up
on_screen_text: 2,697 at fiscal year-end · one square = one store

beats.narration: And yet the same company brought in more than $147 billion in sales.
beats.visual: $147.6B counter beside the tiny $1.28

beats.narration: Tiny margins. Enormous numbers. How does that business actually work?
beats.visual: A tiny pulsing coin vs a growing stack of crates
on_screen_text: How does that business actually work?

beats.narration: Start with the scale, because it changes everything.
beats.visual: Camera pulls back from one storefront to a grid of 49 stores

beats.narration: In the fiscal year that ended in January 2026, Kroger reported $147.6 billion in sales. Its operating profit was $1.9 billion, or 1.28 percent of sales.
beats.visual: A $147.6B column of crates; a thin green sliver on top is circled

beats.narration: That year included a $2.5 billion charge tied to its automated fulfillment network. The year before, operating profit was 2.62 percent of sales.
beats.visual: Red card for the charge; FY2025 vs FY2024 margin bars

beats.narration: Either way, the pattern is the same: one or two cents of operating profit on each dollar, multiplied across a mountain of sales.
beats.visual: 100-dot grid (cents in a dollar); two dots light green

beats.narration: Even one percent of nearly $150 billion is well over a billion dollars.
beats.visual: Equation builds term by term

beats.narration: Scale works the same way at the top of the industry. Walmart's operating income was 4.2 percent of net sales in its latest fiscal year. On more than $700 billion of net sales, that came to nearly $30 billion.
beats.visual: Supercenter storefront; net-sales bar with a 4.2% green slice

beats.narration: That is the first secret of the supermarket. It is not built to earn a lot on each sale. It is built to make an enormous number of them.
beats.visual: Four checkout belts running at once
on_screen_text: Not a lot per sale. An enormous number of sales.

beats.narration: To see where the rest goes, follow a hundred dollars of Kroger's sales through its income statement.
beats.visual: 100 one-dollar coins on the left; waterfall starts with the $100 sales bar

beats.narration: First, the cost of the goods themselves, including advertising, warehousing and transportation. That takes about $77.14.
beats.visual: 77 coins fly into the 'Cost of goods' row; red bar grows

beats.narration: What remains is gross profit: $22.86. Kroger reports a gross margin of 22.9 percent.
beats.visual: Gross profit row appears

beats.narration: Gross margin is what survives the cost of the product. It is not profit yet.
beats.visual: Stamp on the gross-profit row

beats.narration: Next comes the cost of running the business: wages and benefits, utilities, rent, depreciation, and that year's $2.5 billion charge. Together, about $21.58.
beats.visual: 22 coins fly into 'Running the business'; cost chips appear on the spoken words

beats.narration: What's left is operating profit, what the business itself earned: $1.28.
beats.visual: Last coin pulses green; operating-profit sliver

beats.narration: Then interest, taxes and other items. Net earnings, the bottom line for shareholders, came to about 69 cents.
beats.visual: Interest/taxes row and net earnings

beats.narration: Gross margin, operating margin, net margin. Three different numbers that answer three different questions, and mixing them up is the easiest way to misread a supermarket.
beats.visual: Three cards land on the words gross / operating / net

beats.narration: Inside those averages, every product plays a different role. Here is a hypothetical basket. These prices and costs are illustrative, not data from any real store.
beats.visual: ILLUSTRATIVE banner; checkout scans the ten basket items

beats.narration: Ten items, $54 at the register.
beats.visual: Receipt prints as the tenth item scans; register reads $54.00

beats.narration: In this example, the milk earns almost nothing. Stores sometimes price staples like this aggressively, even as loss leaders, sold at a thin margin or below cost to bring shoppers through the door.
beats.visual: Milk close-up with a price-vs-cost bar
on_screen_text: Loss leader: a thin margin, or even below cost, to bring shoppers in

beats.narration: The store-brand cereal earns more than the national brand sitting next to it. The prepared meal from the deli earns more still.
beats.visual: National vs store-brand cereal side by side on a shelf; deli meal pops in

beats.narration: Add it up, and this basket's gross margin lands near 23 percent. We chose the numbers so it would roughly match Kroger's reported figure.
beats.visual: Basket profit waterfall built item by item; total column
on_screen_text: gross margin on $54.00: $12.55 after product costs
Numbers chosen to land near Kroger's reported 22.9%

beats.narration: The point is that a supermarket does not need every item to be profitable. It needs the mix of what you buy to be.
beats.visual: High-margin items outlined in the waterfall
on_screen_text: The mix has to be profitable, not every item

beats.narration: The second secret is speed.
beats.visual: Speed streaks

beats.narration: Much of what a grocery store sells can spoil, so it cannot sit for long. Trucks arrive, pallets move through the stockroom, shelves are refilled, and the same shelf space is emptied again.
beats.visual: Perishables with clocks, then one tracking shot: truck backs in → pallet through the stockroom → shelf refills → shoppers empty it
on_screen_text: Perishable: it can't sit for long

beats.narration: One way to measure this is inventory turnover: the cost of the goods sold in a year, divided by the average inventory on hand.
beats.visual: Goods flow over a fraction bar; a small stock sits under it
on_screen_text: cost of goods sold in a year

beats.narration: Using figures from their latest annual reports, Kroger's inventory turned over roughly twelve times, or about once a month. Costco's turned about fourteen times. Walmart's, with far more general merchandise, about nine times.
beats.visual: Three lanes count laps for one simulated year

beats.narration: Twelve turns a year means the average item spends about a month between the delivery truck and the checkout. The faster that cycle runs, the less cash sits on the shelves at any moment.
beats.visual: 30-day calendar lights up day by day from truck to scanner
on_screen_text: 12 turns a year ≈ about a month from truck to checkout
less cash sitting on the shelves

beats.narration: Every turn is another chance to earn that thin margin again, from the same shelf space and the same money tied up in stock.
beats.visual: A coin loops Truck → Shelf → Checkout; turn counter increments
on_screen_text: +N turns, each one earning the thin margin again
Same shelf space. Same money tied up in stock.

beats.narration: And this is where it gets interesting. At the end of their latest fiscal years, Walmart, Costco and Kroger each owed more in accounts payable than the value of the inventory on their books.
beats.visual: Three balance scales tip toward payables

beats.narration: Accounts payable are bills that haven't been paid yet. When goods sell before their invoices come due, suppliers are, in effect, helping to finance the shelves.
beats.visual: Stack of invoices stamped NOT YET PAID
on_screen_text: Accounts payable = bills not paid yet
…suppliers are, in effect, helping finance the shelves

beats.narration: Here is a simple hypothetical. A case of pasta arrives on day one, sells out within three weeks, and the supplier's invoice is due on day thirty. For more than a week, the store holds the shoppers' money before it pays for the pasta.
beats.visual: ILLUSTRATIVE 30-day timeline: truck drops a pasta case on day 1, shelf empties by day 21, till fills, invoice paid on day 30

beats.narration: Money also flows the other way. Walmart's annual report describes payments from suppliers for volume incentives, warehouse allowances, markdowns and certain advertising, and records them as a reduction of its cost of sales.
beats.visual: Arrows from a supplier warehouse to a store, one per spoken payment type
on_screen_text: → booked as a reduction of cost of sales

beats.narration: So the gross margin you see is shaped not only by shelf prices, but by negotiations most shoppers never see.
beats.visual: A shelf darkens to reveal two contracts behind it
on_screen_text: The shelf price is only part of the story
Gross margin is also shaped by negotiations shoppers never see

beats.narration: Then there is the store's own brand.
beats.visual: Dolly down a supermarket aisle

beats.narration: Kroger says its Our Brands products made up more than $39 billion of its sales in fiscal 2025, and that its supermarkets stock, on average, more than 13,000 private label items.
beats.visual: Shelf with store-brand facings lit by a sweeping spotlight; counters
on_screen_text: 13,000+ private-label items in an average Kroger supermarket

beats.narration: That is roughly a quarter of all its sales.
beats.visual: Pie fills to 26.4%

beats.narration: Costco says its Kirkland Signature products are generally priced lower than national brands, and generally earn higher margins.
beats.visual: Store-brand box; two verbatim Costco 10-K phrases slide in
on_screen_text: “prices that are generally lower than national brands”

beats.narration: Both can be true at once. When the retailer controls the product, the label and the price, it can charge the shopper less and still keep a larger share of each sale.
beats.visual: Conceptual stacked bars: national brand (product, brand owner, store) vs store brand (product, store)
on_screen_text: Conceptual diagram: bar lengths are not data

beats.narration: Now the danger. In a business this thin, small losses are big problems.
beats.visual: Aisle under a pulsing red alert
on_screen_text: In a business this thin, small losses are big problems

beats.narration: Retailers call it shrink: products that were paid for but never sold, because they spoiled, were damaged, were stolen, or simply went missing in the records.
beats.visual: Four panels acted out on the words: banana browns, box crushes, coffee vanishes, records mismatch
on_screen_text: Shrink: paid for, but never sold

beats.narration: Groceries carry extra risk because so much of the store is perishable. The U.S. Department of Agriculture estimated that food losses at the retail level equaled 10 percent of the available food supply in 2010. It is an older estimate, but it shows the scale.
beats.visual: Ten produce crates; one turns red
on_screen_text: 10% of the U.S. food supply was lost at the retail level in 2010
(43 billion pounds) · older estimate; USDA notes some users consider it high

beats.narration: That is also why perishables get marked down near the end of their shelf life. A bag of salad sold at half price still recovers part of its cost. One thrown away recovers nothing.
beats.visual: Salad marked 50% returns coins; a spoiled one drops into a bin

beats.narration: Here is why it matters so much. Imagine a store with a 2 percent operating margin. To make up for one dollar of product lost to shrink, it needs about fifty dollars of new sales.
beats.visual: ILLUSTRATIVE: a $1 hole fills as 50 one-dollar sales ring up
on_screen_text: $1 lost ÷ 2¢ of profit per $1 of sales = $50 of sales

beats.narration: That is why Kroger listed lower shrink among the reasons its gross margin improved last year.
beats.visual: Kroger's reasons list with 'lower shrink' highlighted beside a shelf
on_screen_text: Why Kroger's gross margin rose to 22.9%

beats.narration: Not every company that sells groceries plays the same game.
beats.visual: Three storefronts drop in

beats.narration: Walmart is a general merchandise giant. In its latest fiscal year, grocery was about 59 percent of Walmart U.S. sales. Its consolidated gross profit was 24.2 percent of net sales, and operating income was 4.2 percent.
beats.visual: Supercenter; grocery pie 59%; figures on the words
on_screen_text: 59% of Walmart U.S. sales were grocery

beats.narration: Costco runs membership warehouse clubs. Its gross margin on net sales was just 11.09 percent. But it also collected $5.9 billion in membership fees.
beats.visual: Warehouse club; membership card flies in

beats.narration: Those fees were equal to about half of Costco's operating income for the year. Its model pairs very thin margins on goods with a fee that members pay to shop.
beats.visual: Fees bar inside the operating-income bar

beats.narration: A traditional supermarket chain like Kroger leans on fresh food, its own brands, pharmacy, fuel and growing side businesses such as advertising.
beats.visual: Supermarket storefront; chips appear on the spoken words

beats.narration: So these numbers are not interchangeable. A 24 percent gross margin at Walmart and an 11 percent gross margin at Costco describe different businesses, not better or worse ones.
beats.visual: Two pies (24% vs 11%) with ≠
on_screen_text: Different businesses, not better or worse ones

scenes.title: Payoff
scenes.chapter: So how do they make money?

beats.narration: So, how do supermarkets make money on tiny margins?
beats.visual: Back at the checkout
on_screen_text: So how do supermarkets make money on tiny margins?

beats.narration: By selling an enormous volume. By turning their inventory over again and again. By using supplier credit to help finance their shelves. By leaning on their own brands. By fighting shrink, one damaged box at a time. And, in some models, by charging for membership or selling advertising.
beats.visual: Six lever tiles tick green on the spoken words

beats.narration: The next time you hand over that hundred dollars, remember: at a chain like Kroger, the company keeps only about one to three dollars as operating profit. The rest pays for the food, the people, the buildings and the trucks that make a supermarket work.
beats.visual: The $100 bill splits into a bar: food / people · stores · trucks / kept
on_screen_text: $1–3 kept as operating profit at a chain like Kroger
